question: What exactly does the Go race detector flag?
options: Any concurrency bug, including deadlocks and goroutine leaks
Two goroutines accessing the same memory with no happens-before ordering where at least one access is a write
Any time two goroutines run at the same time
Slow code paths under high concurrency
explanation: The detector reports data races: an unordered pair of accesses to the same memory location where at least one is a write. It does not catch logical race conditions, deadlocks, or goroutine leaks.

question: Which statement about the race detector's guarantees is correct?
options: It can produce false positives, so some reports can be ignored
It has no false positives but can have false negatives — it only catches races on the interleavings actually executed
A clean -race run proves the program is race-free
It statically analyzes all code paths at compile time
explanation: ThreadSanitizer has no false positives — every reported race is real, so never suppress it. But it is dynamic, so it can miss races on paths or interleavings that were never exercised. A clean run only proves the executed paths were clean, which is why coverage and stress tests matter.

options: The race detector has false positives, so it was wrong
The racy interleaving and code path were never exercised during the instrumented test run (a false negative)
Maps are always safe for concurrent use in Go
go test -race only checks the main package
explanation: The detector is dynamic and only finds races on executed interleavings. If the tests never drove concurrent GetOrLoad calls on the same key, the concurrent map access was never observed. Concurrency stress tests are needed to exercise such paths and surface the race.

question: You run `go run -race` on a program where two goroutines each do counter++ without synchronization. What is the most accurate result?
options: It always prints the correct total with no warning
It prints some counter value plus a WARNING: DATA RACE report and exits with a non-zero status
It refuses to compile
It prints the correct total but warns it might be slow
explanation: The program compiles and runs, prints some counter value, AND prints a DATA RACE warning with two stack traces; the process exits with a non-zero status (66 by default) because a race was found. counter++ is an unsynchronized read-modify-write across goroutines.

question: How does ThreadSanitizer decide two accesses form a data race?
options: It counts how many goroutines are running and flags any number above one
It keeps per-goroutine vector clocks and per-word shadow state; if two conflicting accesses have incomparable (concurrent) clocks and at least one is a write, it reports a race
It measures wall-clock time between accesses and flags close ones
It scans the source for the word 'go' before a variable access
explanation: TSan maintains per-goroutine vector clocks that advance at synchronization events, plus shadow memory recording recent accesses per word. When a new access has a clock incomparable with a prior conflicting access (so they are unordered/concurrent) and at least one is a write, it reports a race with both stack traces.

question: Why is the race detector run in tests/CI/load tests rather than normal production?
options: It changes program behavior, so results would be wrong in production
It adds roughly 5-10x CPU and memory overhead and about 2x binary size, which is impractical for normal traffic
It only works on Linux
It requires the source code to be recompiled on every request
explanation: Instrumenting every memory access costs roughly 5-10x CPU and memory and about 2x binary size, so a -race build is confined to tests, CI, and bounded load tests or short-lived canaries rather than normal production traffic.
